claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low strength.
Its relatively low hardness and strength are governed by limited lattice distortion.
Its relatively low hardness and strength are governed by the absence of precipitates in the single-phase solid-solution state.
Limited lattice distortion and absence of precipitates leave dislocation glide only moderately impeded.
Moderately impeded dislocation glide explains the alloy's favorable plasticity.
Moderately impeded dislocation glide explains the alloy's machinability.
Other multicomponent HEAs with greater lattice distortion exhibit higher hardness and compressive strength.
Other multicomponent HEAs containing precipitate interfaces exhibit higher hardness and compressive strength.
The starting equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is an as-cast or fully solutionized single-phase solid solution.
The starting alloy has moderate lattice mismatch among its constituents.
The starting alloy contains no secondary precipitates.
Controlled aging or solute redistribution can increase local lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi.
Controlled aging or minor alloying can form nanoscale coherent precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
Greater lattice distortion or precipitate formation introduces additional barriers to dislocation motion.
The additional barriers to dislocation motion will increase hardness.
The additional barriers to dislocation motion will increase compressive strength.
The additional barriers to dislocation motion will reduce ductility.
Treated samples will have greater hardness and compressive strength than untreated CoCrFeNiTi.
Treated samples will have lower plastic strain at 600 °C than untreated CoCrFeNiTi.

contradictions.description: The intervention is intended to form a second-phase precipitate population, whereas the stated boundary says the hypothesis applies to alloys processed to maintain a single-phase solid solution and may not apply to intentionally multiphase alloys.
